claims.text: The as-built additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has an fcc matrix.
The starting microstructure is uniform and contains minimal preexisting oxide or void content.
Elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing gases causes diffusion-mediated formation of a continuous brittle oxide phase along grain boundaries.
The grain-boundary oxide phase formed under oxidizing conditions is likely composed of Ti and/or Cr oxides.
Intergranular oxide formation reduces grain-boundary cohesion.
Brittle oxide penetration along or across grain boundaries reduces ductility and accelerates crack propagation.
Exposure to a reducing atmosphere induces internal void formation.
The absence of a protective oxide layer in reducing atmospheres favors internal void formation through differential diffusion.
Internal void formation under reducing conditions weakens grain-boundary cohesion.
Compromising grain-boundary integrity through either intergranular oxidation or void formation accelerates degradation and can cause catastrophic failure.
Oxidizing exposure will increase intergranular oxide thickness relative to the as-built state.
Oxidizing exposure will reduce fracture toughness and tensile ductility relative to the as-built state.
Reducing exposure will increase internal porosity or void density relative to the starting state.
Reducing exposure will degrade mechanical integrity.
Elevated temperature can increase atomic mobility and alter mechanical behavior in high-entropy alloys.
The proposed intergranular oxidation and void-nucleation mechanisms become applicable above approximately 700 °C when exposure is sufficiently long for diffusion-controlled reactions.
The general role of diffusion-mediated intergranular degradation is supported by the cited prior evidence.

contradictions.description: The baseline and predicted outcomes use the unexposed as-built state, whereas the falsification experiment uses a specimen exposed to 800 °C in an inert atmosphere as the baseline. These controls are not equivalent because inert high-temperature exposure can itself alter microstructure and mechanical properties.
